result.question:
Investigate the August 2026 Trezor Google-Ads phishing incident and the wider "Google Sites as phishing host in Google Search sponsored results" attack class. Anchor facts already established (do not re-derive, build on them): On 2026-08-06 19:56 UTC X user @ReallyBadDay99 ("David") posted that he lost his life savings after clicking the TOP SPONSORED Google result for the query "Trezor wallet"; the scam page was hosted at https://sites.google.com/view/start-trezor-suite and harvested wallet recovery seed phrases; he named harvesting Bitcoin address bc1qrz33mr7tx8wrpcs2pxrvv83hqwpm907s9shkz4 and tagged @zachxbt and @CertiK. @BitcoinNewsCom amplified it 2026-08-07 14:26 UTC. That BTC address has received 24.0413582 BTC across 80 deposits and been swept nearly empty. The sites.google.com URL now redirects to a Google sign-in (unpublished or removed).

Research angles needed:
1. INCIDENT: All reporting, Trezor's official statements/responses, ZachXBT or CertiK or Scam Sniffer or SEAL (Security Alliance) analysis of this specific case, victim reports, total losses, whether Google responded or commented. Any other victims of start-trezor-suite specifically.
2. THE google.com DISPLAY-URL MECHANIC: Precisely how Google Ads determines the displayed/visible URL of a search ad, and how hosting a phishing page on sites.google.com (or other Google-owned properties like Google Sites, Looker Studio, Google Groups, Firebase, appspot.com, Blogger, Google Docs/Drive) causes the ad to display a google.com domain. Google Ads destination-requirement policy, display URL vs final URL rules, and why a google.com display URL passes ad review and looks trustworthy. Any Google policy documentation on this.
3. ADVERTISER ACCOUNT MECHANICS: How attackers obtain and operate the Google Ads accounts that run these — hijacked/compromised advertiser accounts, aged accounts bought on markets, agency/MCC abuse, payment-method abuse, the "advertiser verification" and advertiser identity requirements, and how the Google Ads Transparency Center exposes (or fails to expose) the real advertiser. Documented cases of the advertiser names used in crypto phishing ads.
4. CLOAKING + GEO-TARGETING TRADECRAFT: How these campaigns evade Google's ad review — cloaking services, geo/IP filtering, residential proxy detection, device targeting, ad-schedule tricks, click-tracker redirect chains, doorway/intermediate redirects. Which countries these campaigns typically target and why targeting differs by geo.
5. PRIOR ART / PATTERN: Prior documented Google Sites and google.com-subdomain phishing campaigns against hardware wallets and crypto brands (Trezor, Ledger, Exodus, Phantom, MetaMask, Uniswap), including the May 2026 Uniswap Google Ads phishing case, the SEAL figure of 356+ malicious ad links and $1.27M losses since March 2026, seed-phrase harvesting kits, and how long such pages typically stay up before Google removes them. Also any known takedown/abuse-report path and its latency.

Prioritise primary sources: Trezor's own blog/X account, Google's published policy pages, security-vendor writeups (Malwarebytes, Scam Sniffer, SEAL, Check Point, Sophos, Bleeping Computer), on-chain analysts. Report exact dates, exact URLs, exact dollar figures, exact advertiser names, and exact policy wording where available. Flag clearly anything that is claim-only versus confirmed.
result.summary: The August 2026 Trezor incident is documentarily real but evidentially thin at its centre: the originating post (2026-08-06 19:56:03 UTC) is confirmed verbatim through X's own syndication API — naming the top-sponsored "Trezor wallet" result, https://sites.google.com/view/start-trezor-suite, and address bc1qrz33mr7tx8wrpcs2pxrvv83hqwpm907s9shkz4 — yet it was posted from an account created 16 minutes and 15 seconds earlier, so "life savings" and "top sponsored placement" remain uncorroborated claims, while the URL and the on-chain address are the durable, checkable artifacts. Trezor officially acknowledged it 15h02m later (2026-08-07 10:57:56 UTC), saying it was "escalating this internally and reporting the phishing page through the relevant channels", followed by a standalone advisory at 12:24:04 UTC; no Google statement was located. The attack class is well-documented prior art: SEAL Intel's 13–30 March 2026 report records 351–356 blocked malicious Google Ads URLs, $810,929 confirmed and $1,274,259 total stolen, and describes sites.google.com/view/ pages (plus docs.google.com and business.google.com) used as the "Primary" web frame so the sponsored result renders "in an extremely convincing way — together with proper title, description and a logo", with cloaked secondary iframes delivering the cloned front end. On accountability, Google's own policy pages confirm advertiser verification is a gradual, selective rollout that does not gate ad serving ("You can still run ads if you don't complete advertiser verification"), and that verified advertisers' names, locations, creatives and serving dates surface in the Ads Transparency Center — a mechanism that exposes only the self-declared identity, which in documented cases has been fabricated. Critically, the single most-repeated technical explanation for this attack class — that hosting on sites.google.com makes the ad legitimately display a trusted "google.com" URL because display and final URL share the google.com root — FAILED verification in every form it was tested and must not be repeated as fact.

findings.claim: The originating report is authentic and its contents are exactly as recorded: posted 2026-08-06T19:56:03Z by @ReallyBadDay99 ('David'), it names the top sponsored Google result for 'Trezor wallet' as a phishing site, links (via t.co) to expanded_url https://sites.google.com/view/start-trezor-suite, names harvesting address bc1qrz33mr7tx8wrpcs2pxrvv83hqwpm907s9shkz4, and tags @Trezor, @zachxbt and @CertiK. Every substantive assertion inside it — top-sponsored placement, 'life savings', 'vacuuming up millions' — is the poster's own uncorroborated claim.
findings.evidence: Verbatim text via X's first-party syndication API (HTTP 200, 3,129 bytes): "Hey @Trezor, just lost my life savings. Top sponsored Google result for 'Trezor wallet' is a phishing site! The scam page (https://t.co/z5s9HaJIu2) is vacuuming up millions. Harvesting address is currently sitting at: bc1qrz33mr7tx8wrpcs2pxrvv83hqwpm907s9shkz4 @zachxbt @CertiK". created_at = 2026-08-06T19:56:03.000Z; entities.urls expanded_url = https://sites.google.com/view/start-trezor-suite; user_mentions = Trezor (1431204614), zachxbt (3012852462), CertiK (993673575230996480); isEdited=False with a single edit_tweet_id, so 'verbatim' is safe. Authenticated by a third party: the blue-verified @Trezor account replied with in_reply_to_status_id_str = 2085454877719675354. Corroborating caution: no media/screenshot is attached (JSON carries no media keys), so SERP placement is unevidenced in the source; crypto.news states "the value of David's loss, the total amount allegedly stolen from other users, and the address's connection to the phishing website had not been independently verified at the time of publication", and every outlet hedges with 'claims'/'says'. The reported on-chain aggregate (~24.04 BTC / 80 deposits ≈ $1.6M at ~$65,172) is ONE million spread across many victims, so 'vacuuming up millions' is not corroborated. The victim testimony therefore has zero account history behind it and must be treated as claim-only; the checkable elements of this incident are the URL, the crawler-captured page title and the BTC address, not the person.

findings.evidence: Live re-fetch on 2026-08-09 returns a user object byte-identical to the recorded capture: "id_str":"2085450786406862848","name":"David","screen_name":"ReallyBadDay99","is_blue_verified":false,"verified":false,"profile_image_url_https":"https://abs.twimg.com/sticky/default_profile_images/default_profile_normal.png". Snowflake decode (id>>22 + epoch 1288834974657) gives a 975.445 s delta = 16m15.44s; structural cross-check status_id − user_id = 4,091,312,812,506 = exactly 975,445 ms of snowflake time. Method validated three ways: (a) the status-ID decode matches X's own created_at to sub-second; (b) CertiK's user ID 993673575230996480 decodes to May 2018, matching CertiK's public 'Joined May 2018', proving user-ID snowflake decoding recovers true account creation; (c) pre-snowflake sequential IDs (jack=12, elonmusk=44196397, Trezor=1431204614, zachxbt=3012852462) are 9–18 orders of magnitude smaller, ruling out a legacy-ID misread. Caveat carried forward: 'throwaway' is an inference — a 16-minute-old account is equally consistent with a genuine large holder opening a burner rather than doxxing himself. The post carries real engagement (1,486 likes, 252 replies). The same API response carries card domain "sites.google.com" and crawler-captured title "Trezor Hardware Wallet (Official) | Bitcoin & Crypto Security | Trezor"; a separate attempt to use the card's media-ID timestamp (2085757634972717056 → 2026-08-07T15:59:06Z) to bound Google's takedown latency was REFUTED and must not be used.

findings.claim: Trezor officially acknowledged the incident at 2026-08-07 10:57:56 UTC — a reply from the verified @Trezor account to the victim's 2026-08-06 19:56:03 UTC post, i.e. 15h01m53s later — stating it was escalating internally and reporting the phishing page through 'the relevant channels', and followed 86 minutes afterwards at 12:24:04 UTC with a standalone advisory about fake Trezor sites in sponsored results. This establishes that the vendor itself initiated a takedown request; it does NOT date a measurable takedown latency.
findings.vote: 3-0 on the acknowledgment; 2-1 on the escalation/takedown-clock framing
findings.evidence: Full reply text, reproduced word-for-word by cryptotimes.io: "Hi David, We're deeply sorry to hear this. Thank you for flagging the site and address. We're escalating this internally and reporting the phishing page through the relevant channels. Please contact our Support team as soon as possible and share the details of what happened:…". Timestamp verified deterministically: snowflake decode of 2085681844599546144 = 2026-08-07T10:57:56.504Z, exactly matching the stated created_at; the victim post decodes to 2026-08-06T19:56:03.383Z, giving 15h01m53s. Independent corroboration of the ACTION, not just the words, from BeInCrypto via tech.yahoo.com: "The team escalated the case internally and reported the page for takedown"; criptonoticias.com carries the Spanish rendering ("Estamos escalando esto internamente y reportando la página"). The 'earlier advisory' some summaries reference is actually LATER: Trezor's broad statement "We're seeing an increase in phishing websites impersonating Trezor, including fake sites appearing in sponsored search results" has ID 2085703519776936294 = 2026-08-07T12:24:04.269Z, so the 10:57:56 reply is Trezor's first public response. OVERREACH TO AVOID: the timestamp records when Trezor publicly SAID it was reporting, not when a report was filed; crypto.news notes Trezor "did not say whether the specific Google Sites page identified in David's post had been removed", so 10:57 UTC is only an upper bound on when reporting began. Trezor said 'the relevant channels' and never named Google; nothing establishes that Google separately initiated a takedown. Limitation: x.com returns HTTP 402 to direct fetch from this box, so the primary rests on ID arithmetic plus three secondary outlets.

findings.claim: Google Ads advertiser verification is a selective, rolling programme and NOT a precondition to serving search ads — accounts are notified after the fact with a deadline, and Google explicitly states unverified advertisers can still run ads. This leaves a structural window in which an unverified advertiser account serves live search ads.
findings.evidence: answer/9703665 states verbatim: "As a part of a gradual rollout of Google's transparency efforts, all advertisers will eventually be required to complete advertiser verification"; "Google Ads will notify you via an in-account notification or an email when you need to complete advertiser verification and what your deadline will be"; and "When your account is selected for verification, some of your ads may be restricted" — 'eventually', 'gradual rollout', 'selected' and 'some' all indicate a non-universal gate. answer/15577076 states directly: "You can still run ads if you don't complete advertiser verification" and "No deadline? You may choose to get verified on your own." answer/15588490 confirms pausing follows only a MISSED deadline, i.e. ads serve first. Second primary surface: the Google Ads API docs state "An empty response indicates that the customer account is not required to undergo advertiser identity verification" and "You can also proactively undergo verification without being required to do so" — dispositive that verification is not universal. Currency checked: the only 2026 change found is cosmetic (Advertiser Verification moved under the Account section, Jan 2026 — 'No status change — just a UI shift'); the June 2026 financial-services verification across 24 new EEA markets has 'rolling enforcement beginning July 23, 2026', itself rolling. Fair qualification: a legitimate crypto hardware-wallet advertiser separately needs restricted-financial-products CERTIFICATION before serving in approved markets — a distinct programme this finding does not cover. Two related claims (that brand-term bidding and that financial services are named verification triggers) were REFUTED 0-3 and must not be repeated.

findings.claim: Once an advertiser is verified, Google publicly discloses the advertiser's name/organization and location, name-change history, ad creatives, dates and locations ads served, whether ads were removed or the account suspended, and organization contact information — via ad disclosures and the Ads Transparency Center. This is the documented mechanism by which the advertiser behind a phishing ad can in principle be identified after the fact, but it surfaces only the self-declared identity.
findings.evidence: Raw fetch of answer/9703665 (2026-08-09, 1,608,659 bytes) contains, under 'How will my information be used? Google will use your information to:', the verbatim bullet "Show an ad disclosure, which will include your name or organization's name and location", then 'Some of your account information will also be publicly available, including:' → "Name change history", "Ad creatives", "Dates and locations ads served", "Ads removed or accounts suspended for legal or policy reasons", "Organization contact information". Independent primary corroboration from answer/13733850: "In the Ads Transparency Center and in ad disclosures, Google will show advertiser information such as the advertiser name, location, the entity that pays for the ads, and the ads they have served over a certain time period for all advertisers serving ads on Google" and "For advertisers who are verified, Google will display the advertiser's legal name, or trademark name and location as provided by the advertiser via the verification program". Both pages returned HTTP 200 live on 2026-08-09. CRITICAL LIMITATION: the disclosed identity is self-declared and can be fabricated — Malwarebytes' July 2024 fake Google Authenticator search ad ran under advertiser 'Larry Marr', of whom the writeup says "The truth is Larry Marr has nothing to do with Google, and is likely a fake account." Two of the six items have thin public surfaces: the linked 'Ads transparency' page contains no occurrence of 'removed', 'suspend' or 'name change' (grep-verified), and its EEA-only extras are limited to targeting information, total recipients and subject-matter label; the only removed-ads repository located is 'Ads we removed in Europe' (DSA-scoped, not fetchable here — Google served /sorry/ to this datacenter IP). Retention (~1 year from last display, longer in the EU) is secondary-source only and unverified; a Google Ads Community thread reports removed ads still showing in ATC, contradicting the claim that suspended advertisers vanish.

findings.claim: SEAL (Security Alliance) Intel documented this exact attack class four months earlier: a malicious Google Ads crypto campaign wave over 13–30 March 2026 covering 351–356 blocked malicious ad URLs, with $810,929 in confirmed stolen funds and $1,274,259 total including unattributable losses. The report is internally inconsistent on the count (351 in prose, 'over 356' in a second prose line, 356 entries in the dataset header); the widely-cited '356+ links / $1.27M' figure traces to this page.
findings.evidence: Direct fetch of the primary (SEAL Intel, published 2026-04-21, '27 min read') confirms all four figures verbatim: "In recent weeks SEAL successfully blocked 351 malicious Google Ads URLs via Eth-Phishing-Detect"; dataset header "356 entries · Mar 13–30, 2026 · Source: SEAL Phishing Bot"; "Confirmed funds stolen (Total): $810,929"; "Total funds stolen in the period of March 13th to March 30th (Including confirmed and unattributable): $1,274,259". A THIRD inconsistent count exists that the claim understates: "In the recent few weeks, we successfully blocked over 356 malicious advertisement URLs". Impersonated-brand split: Uniswap 41%, Morpho 31%. SEAL's own conservative-bias caveat: "Reliable attribution of value loss to a specific advertisement is only possible when we are in direct contact with the victim and they can provide the requested indicators of compromise. Consequently, the actual total amount of stolen funds is considerably greater" — bias runs toward under-statement. Secondary press (cybersecuritynews.com, gbhackers.com, cryptika.com, bitcoinfoundation.org) garbles the scoping as '356 links blocked over the past year', conflating the block count with a separate SEAL line about 'a steady volume of attacker-deployed Google Ads each week for more than a year' — do not repeat that framing. Figures are self-reported and unaudited: cite as 'SEAL documented', and prefer '351–356 (report inconsistent)' to a bare 356. No source disputing or revising the figures was found.

findings.claim: The mechanic is Google-property hosting: SEAL documents sites.google.com/view/ pages used as the 'Primary' web frame, plus docs.google.com and business.google.com, with the cloned front end and payloads delivered through secondary iframes paired with fingerprinting and cloaking scripts. The Google-hosted entry page is what lets the sponsored result render convincingly and pass ad review — the same hosting pattern as the August 2026 sites.google.com/view/start-trezor-suite page.
findings.evidence: SEAL states: "One of the popular methods is utilizing high-reputation URLs as a 'Primary' web frame", naming sites.google.com, docs.google.com and business.google.com, with the concrete example URL "sites.google.com/view/ads-unisw-x1/", and concludes "In Google Search interface, the URL is displayed in an extremely convincing way - together with proper title, description and a logo." Independent corroboration of the causal link from cybersecuritynews.com (2026-04-22): "The ad links to a page hosted on trusted Google-owned domains like sites.google.com or docs.google.com, which allows it to pass Google's review process since the initial URL appears completely safe." The Trezor bridge holds: the August page is confirmed Google Sites-hosted by crypto.news, cryptotimes.io and @BitcoinNewsCom ('The phishing page, hosted on Google Sites'), and follows the identical sites.google.com/view/ pattern as SEAL's ads-unisw-x1 example. CAVEATS: (1) hosting determines only the display URL — the headline and description come from the advertiser's ad copy and the icon from the advertiser's logo asset/favicon — so SEAL's bundling of 'title, description and logo' with hosting over-attributes, and this finding mirrors rather than exceeds its source; (2) the Google Sites page is the ENTRY FRAME only, with payloads served from separate infrastructure (Cloudflare Workers, Arweave) and non-targeted visitors sent to benign pages, so 'landing page hosted on a Google property' is true of the frame, not the whole stack; (3) whether the Trezor ad specifically rendered a visible google.com display URL is claim-level from the victim/reporting, not documented by SEAL. Searches for an alternative explanation (display-URL spoofing showing uniswap.org/trezor.io) found no supporting source; coverage of the May 2026 Uniswap case (Scam Sniffer / b-block, 2026-05-25, ~$400K, two attacker wallets on Etherscan) describes cloned front-ends reached via sponsored results and does not contradict Google-property hosting.

result.caveats:
1) THE CORE "DISPLAY URL" MECHANIC IS UNCONFIRMED — this is the biggest hole. Every formulation of the most-repeated technical explanation was tested against support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16428020 and answer/6368661 and REFUTED: that the destination-mismatch rule lets a sites.google.com landing page legitimately display "google.com" (votes 0-3 and 1-2), that google.com is treated purely as a matchable domain string (0-3), that the shared-hosting subdomain clause fails to catch path-based Google Sites URLs (0-3), and that the trust abuse is a structural consequence of a compliant rule rather than a circumvention (0-3). Do NOT state as fact that hosting on sites.google.com causes the ad to show a google.com display URL. Only the general "Google-owned hosting makes the destination look trustworthy and pass review" claim survived, at medium confidence.

2) ADVERTISER-ACCOUNT MECHANICS ARE ESSENTIALLY UNANSWERED for this incident. No advertiser identity for the start-trezor-suite campaign was established. The SEAL-attributed advertiser names (ADOLFO ARIEL CASTILLO VERGARA 84 campaigns / 30.8%, "Apple Inc." 83 / 30.4%, AD Taxi 69 / 25.3%) and the statement that Google suspended all listed accounts were REFUTED 0-3; the Malwarebytes hijacked-advertiser chain (credential + session-cookie theft → add a new admin on a different Gmail → lock out the owner → burn the budget) was also REFUTED 0-3, as was the two-stage "Google Sites page is only a gateway that redirects off-platform" claim. Treat all of these as unverified leads, not findings.

3) CLOAKING TRADECRAFT IS UNVERIFIED. The 1Campaign cloaking-as-a-service claims — including the 0–100 fraud score and automatic blocking of Google/Microsoft/Tencent Cloud/OVH ranges — split 1-2 and did not survive; SEAL's specific TDS detail (non-targeted geo/OS or open devtools redirected to a benign Wikipedia page, traffic routed through thirdtemple.top behind Cloudflare) was REFUTED 0-3. Only the generic "fingerprinting and cloaking scripts + secondary iframes" description survived, inside the medium-confidence hosting finding. No geo-targeting pattern was established at all.

4) NO TAKEDOWN LATENCY IS MEASURABLE. The attempt to bound it from the X card's media snowflake was REFUTED 1-2. We know only that Trezor said it was reporting at 2026-08-07 10:57 UTC and that the URL now redirects to a Google sign-in. Neither the removal time nor the actor who removed it is established, and no documented abuse-report SLA was found.

5) NO GOOGLE STATEMENT was located. No ZachXBT, CertiK, Scam Sniffer or SEAL analysis of THIS incident or of bc1qrz33mr7tx8wrpcs2pxrvv83hqwpm907s9shkz4 was found, and no second victim of start-trezor-suite was identified. The 24.0413582 BTC / 80 deposits figure comes from the task's anchor facts and was not independently re-derived here; the "80 victims" in cryptotimes.io's headline is that deposit count, not 80 confirmed people.

6) SOURCE-ACCESS LIMITS shaped the evidence base. x.com returns HTTP 402 to direct fetch from this box and the xcancel mirror served a browser-verification page, so all X primaries were verified via the syndication API plus deterministic snowflake arithmetic plus secondary outlets; adstransparency.google.com/removed served /sorry/ to this datacenter IP; a SERP probe for "trezor wallet" from a US residential exit hit a CAPTCHA, so the ad itself was never observed by us.

7) TIME-SENSITIVITY: the incident is three days old (2026-08-06 → 2026-08-09) and still developing — loss totals, any Google or ZachXBT response, and on-chain sweeping are all likely to move. SEAL's dataset is from March 2026, four months before the Trezor page, so "same mechanic" is an inference across a four-month gap even though it is corroborated at both ends.

refuted.claim: X's automatically generated link-preview card — a machine-captured artifact of the live page, not the poster's description — records the sites.google.com page's own <title> tag as "Trezor Hardware Wallet (Official) | Bitcoin & Crypto Security | Trezor" under domain sites.google.com. This is independent evidence that the Google-hosted page impersonated Trezor's official site down to the title string (including the word 'Official'), and that the phishing content was served on a google.com domain — the exact mechanic by which such an ad displays a trusted google.com URL. It is also the only surviving copy of the page's metadata now that the URL redirects to Google sign-in.

The phishing page was still live and serving Trezor-impersonating content on 2026-08-07 at ~15:59 UTC — roughly 20 hours after the victim publicly named it and ~1.5 hours after @BitcoinNewsCom amplified it. Derived from the card thumbnail's media snowflake ID 2085757634972717056, which decodes to 2026-08-07T15:59:06Z; X could only have rendered that preview image by successfully crawling the URL at that time. The decoder was validated by a positive control (tweet ID 2085454877719675354 decodes to 2026-08-06T19:56:03Z, matching the stated created_at exactly). This is a hard lower bound on Google's takedown latency for start-trezor-suite. Caveat: the media ID timestamps image creation, so the crawl could in principle be marginally earlier — it cannot be later.

Google Ads' destination-requirements rule that the ad's display URL must share a domain with the final URL is trivially satisfied by hosting the phishing page on sites.google.com, because sites.google.com and ads.google.com share the root domain google.com — so the ad legitimately renders a google.com display URL. This is the exact display-URL mechanic that makes a sponsored result carrying a sites.google.com landing page look like an official Google property.

The sites.google.com page is only a gateway, not the credential-harvesting page itself: clicking the call-to-action on the Google Sites page redirects the victim off-platform to a separately hosted phishing kit. This two-stage structure is what lets the reviewable ad destination remain a clean google.com URL while the harvesting happens elsewhere.

The campaigns are run from hijacked advertiser accounts obtained by phishing Google Ads customers: the kit collects credentials and session cookies, the attacker then adds a new administrator using a different Gmail account, locks the legitimate owner out, and spends the account's budget on further malicious ads — meaning the advertiser identity shown in ads/Transparency Center is a real but compromised third party.

Google Ads' Destination mismatch policy requires the ad's display URL domain to match the domain of the final/mobile URL the user actually lands on — which is precisely why a phishing page hosted on a Google-owned property (e.g. sites.google.com/view/start-trezor-suite) can legitimately display a google.com URL in the sponsored result: there is no mismatch to detect, the display and final domains genuinely agree.

Google's own policy page uses "google.com" as the example display URL in its illustration of a violation (display google.com / final example.com), confirming that google.com is treated by the policy purely as a domain string to be matched, with no special rule barring advertisers from running ads whose display URL is google.com when the landing page is genuinely hosted on google.com.

The policy does contain a shared-hosting clause requiring a subdomain to identify the specific site rather than the parent domain — its worked example is blogspot.com (display) vs mycompany.blogspot.com (final) — but the rule is written around subdomains only, so a path-based Google Sites page (google.com/…/view/start-trezor-suite, no distinguishing subdomain) is not caught by it.

Google Ads' Destination requirements policy makes a display URL that does NOT match the final URL's domain a disapproval-triggering violation — which means a phishing ad landing on sites.google.com/view/start-trezor-suite showing 'google.com' as its display URL is policy-COMPLIANT rather than a policy breach. The trust-signal abuse is a structural consequence of the rule, not a circumvention of it.

The same 'Destination mismatch' section contains a bullet that addresses shared hosting directly — sites must use a subdomain to distinguish themselves from other sites on the same domain — yet Google Sites allocates path-based URLs (sites.google.com/view/<name>) rather than per-user subdomains, so every Google Sites page shares one registrable domain and cannot satisfy this bullet by construction.

A commercial cloaking-as-a-service platform called 1Campaign is sold specifically to help attackers run malicious Google Ads, keep phishing and crypto-drainer landing pages online longer, and evade Google's ad screening — establishing that the evasion layer behind google-ads phishing is a productised, subscription-style service rather than bespoke attacker tooling.

1Campaign assigns every visitor a 0–100 fraud score and automatically blocks traffic originating from Google's own network ranges (alongside Microsoft, Tencent Cloud and OVH) — i.e. Google's ad-review and crawling infrastructure is explicitly named and excluded, which is the mechanism by which a malicious ad passes review while real users see the phishing page.

Running ads on brand-related queries is an explicit trigger for Google Ads advertiser verification — meaning a phishing ad bidding on the brand term "Trezor wallet" falls inside a category Google itself flags for identity checks, so the attacker either passed verification with real/forged identity documents or ran on an account that had already been verified (e.g. a hijacked one).

Financial services is a named industry trigger for advertiser verification, and Google states extra requirements apply to run ads in certain industries — relevant to whether a crypto-wallet-targeting ad should have been gated behind the financial-services verification track before it could serve.

The operators ran a Traffic Detection System with origin-aware cloaking: visitors arriving from a non-targeted geography or operating system, or with developer tools open, were redirected to a benign Wikipedia page instead of the phishing flow, with traffic routed through the attacker-controlled host thirdtemple.top behind Cloudflare.

The Google Ads accounts serving these campaigns were a mix of compromised legitimate advertisers and verified accounts bought on criminal markets; the top three advertiser identities shown in the Ads Transparency data were ADOLFO ARIEL CASTILLO VERGARA (84 campaigns, 30.8%), 'Apple Inc.' (83 campaigns, 30.4%) and AD Taxi (69 campaigns, 25.3%) — i.e. the displayed advertiser identity, including an impersonated 'Apple Inc.', does not identify the real operator. Google suspended all advertiser accounts listed in the report.

Trezor publicly responded to the Google-Ads phishing incident by escalating it internally and filing a takedown report against the fake page — i.e. the vendor, not Google, initiated removal. (Reported by BeInCrypto; no Trezor blog post or embedded official X post is shown in the article, so this is claim-only pending Trezor's own channels.)
